newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh hails water-sharing pact with India.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh hails water-sharing pact with India.

text.p: Bangladesh welcomed on Thursday the signing of a long-awaited treaty with India which tackled the thorny issue of sharing water from the Ganges River.
"This is an historic agreement which brings our two countries' relations back to where they were in 1971-72," Finance Minister S.A.M.S. Kibria told Reuters.
India helped neighbouring Bangladesh gain independence from Pakistan in 1971, but relations had since soured.
Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina and Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda signed the 30-year water-sharing agreement in New Delhi on Thursday.

Bangladesh and a large area of northern India depend on water from the Ganges, which originates in the Himalayas and flows through India before crossing into Bangladesh, where it empties into the Bay of Bengal.
Kibria said Bangladesh was now hopeful of returning economic prosperity to millions of its citizens in the north.
"The negative policies of the past had been harmful and detrimental to the people in the north. We have put that chapter behind us," he said.
The Ganges' water levels vary dramatically, flooding large areas during the monsoon months or falling to dangerously low levels in the January-June dry period.

The two neighbour's decades-old water dispute worsened after India built the Farakka Barrage in 1974, a dam that curbed the flow of the Ganges, which irrigates much of northern India before flowing into Bangladesh.

In 1977, the two nations signed an agreement allowing Bangladesh a guaranteed minimum 34,000 cubic feet of water per second (cusecs) between October and June every year. But the guarantee was dropped in a new six-year accord signed in 1982.

A senior Indian Foreign Ministry official said that under the new treaty, if water flow at the barrage near the border of the two countries falls below 70,000 cusecs, they would split the water evenly.

If the flow is between 70,000 and 75,000 cusecs, Bangladesh will receive 35,000 cusecs and India the balance, the official said. If the flow exceeds 75,000 cusecs, 40,000 would be guaranteed to India and the rest to Bangladesh.
The finance minister said Bangladesh could now draw up long-term water development plans.
"We hope the nation can now move forward with confidence into the 21st century."

Amjad Hossain Khan, former chairman of the Bangladesh Water Development Board, said the agreement on sharing Ganges water was a positive development which would allow the country to prepare its water resources management plan.
"We should start a water resources plan immediately," he told Reuters.
Khan, also a prominent water management expert, said Bangladesh could now start planning a dam of its own at Pangsha, 90 miles (150 km) west of Dhaka.

He said plans for the 1,990-metre (2,170-yard) long dam were first drawn up in 1984. The dam is designed to irrigate 1.35 million hectares of land and protect another 1.44 million hectares from floods, he said.
The treaty was expected to give a political boost to Hasina, who assumed power in June following general elections.
Hasina's Awami League party regained power 21 years after her father, independence leader Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, was assassinated in a bloody military coup in August 1975.
